## Required Library
```r
install.packages("tidyverse")
library(tidyverse)
```

## Syntax

```r
# Pipe style
df %>% pull(column)

# Non-pipe style
pull(df, column)
```
::: {.desc-item}
`pull()` extracts one column from a data frame or tibble and returns it as a vector.
It works a bit like using `$` to extract one column, but it fits more naturally inside a pipe.
:::

```r
df %>% pull(column) %>% mean()
```
::: {.desc-item}
Because `pull()` returns a vector, you can use the result in calculations right away.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## When should you use `pull()`?
Use `pull()` when you want the values from one column, not the full data frame.
It is handy before calculations, summaries, or printing a column as a vector.
Unlike `select()`, which keeps columns in a data frame, `pull()` returns just the values as a vector.
That makes it a good choice when you want to use the result in a calculation.
:::

## Examples

<div class="example-section">
<div class="collapse-toolbar"><button class="collapse-btn">Expand All</button></div>

<details class="example-item">
<summary>Pull one column as a vector</summary>
<div class="example-body">

```{webr}
library(tidyverse)

tablet_weights <- read_csv("data/tablet_weights.csv")

weights <- tablet_weights %>% pull(weight_mg)
weights
```
</div>
</details>

<details class="example-item">
<summary>Use pulled values in a calculation</summary>
<div class="example-body">

```{webr}
library(tidyverse)

tablet_weights <- read_csv("data/tablet_weights.csv")

mean_weight <- tablet_weights %>%
  pull(weight_mg) %>%
  mean()

cat("Mean tablet weight:", round(mean_weight, 1), "mg\n")
```
</div>
</details>

<details class="example-item">
<summary>Pull values for a quick comparison</summary>
<div class="example-body">

```{webr}
library(tidyverse)

tablet_weights <- read_csv("data/tablet_weights.csv")

tablet_weights %>%
  pull(weight_mg) %>%
  range()
```
</div>
</details>

</div>

## Argument Overview
<p class="arg-intro">Required arguments must be included when using a function while optional arguments can be included on demand.</p>

::: {.arg-section}
<div class="collapse-toolbar"><button class="collapse-btn">Expand All</button></div>

<details class="arg-item">
<summary><code>.data</code> <span class="arg-types">data frame | tibble</span> <span class="arg-badge required">Required</span></summary>
<div class="arg-body">
The data frame to pull a column from. In a pipe (`%>%`), this is passed automatically from the left-hand side.

```r
tablet_weights %>% pull(weight_mg)
```

<p class="data-types"><strong>Data Types:</strong> <code>data.frame</code> | <code>tibble</code></p>
</div>
</details>

<details class="arg-item">
<summary><code>var</code> — column to extract <span class="arg-types">column name | position</span> <span class="arg-badge optional">Optional</span></summary>
<div class="arg-body">
The column to extract.
You can use a column name or a numeric position.
If omitted, `pull()` uses the last column.

```r
pull(tablet_weights, weight_mg)
pull(tablet_weights, 3)
```

<p class="data-types"><strong>Data Types:</strong> column name or integer position · Default: last column</p>
</div>
</details>

<details class="arg-item">
<summary><code>name</code> — column to use for names <span class="arg-types">column name | position</span> <span class="arg-badge optional">Optional</span></summary>
<div class="arg-body">
If you want the output vector to have names, supply a second column to use as the names.
If omitted, the returned vector is unnamed.

```r
tablet_weights %>% pull(weight_mg, name = tablet_id)
```

<p class="data-types"><strong>Data Types:</strong> column name or integer position · Default: <code>NULL</code></p>
</div>
</details>
:::
